questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — background job queue (javabootcamp System Design, guide astraupskill/03-SYSTEM-DESIGN.md §4.5; blocks from modules 10, 11, 12 and 13). Requirements: producers submit jobs; workers run each job; jobs survive crashes; failed jobs retry with backoff; some jobs run later or first; a broken job must not block the queue; a job should run once, or at least look as if it did. Write your design before you look: sizing, data model, partitioning, durability and delivery guarantees, failure modes, and the trade-off you would defend. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70 % with every [w3] hit).

keyPoints.text: [w2] Sizing workers with Little's law: jobs in flight = job throughput x job duration, which is the number of workers (or permits) needed.
[w3] Durable enqueue: the job is written as a DB row with an outbox, or appended to a log, so a crash never loses an accepted job.
keyPoints.quote: Durable enqueue via a log or an outbox

keyPoints.text: [w2] Data model follows the sketch: each job carries its run-at time and priority for the scheduler, a lease (visibility timeout) while a worker holds it, and an attempt count that sends it to the dead-letter queue after N failures.
[w3] A crashed worker's lease lapses and the job is redelivered, so delivery is at-least-once and every job needs an idempotency key or dedupe.
keyPoints.quote: which makes delivery at-least-once, so jobs need idempotency keys or dedupe

keyPoints.text: [w2] Partitioning: jobs keyed by tenant or entity and hashed to partitions get per-key ordering and let workers scale out.
keyPoints.quote: Jobs keyed by tenant or entity, hashed to partitions, give per-key ordering

keyPoints.text: [w2] Failures retry with exponential backoff and jitter, then go to a dead-letter queue.
keyPoints.quote: Retries with exponential backoff and jitter, then a dead-letter queue

keyPoints.text: [w3] Visibility-timeout trade-off named: too short and a slow job is redelivered while still running, too long and a crashed worker's job sits idle; heartbeat-extended leases fix both.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the same job queue at 10x the volume, or with workers crashing or a downstream service failing every job. What breaks first, and what in your design already prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] A poison job with no retry cap and no dead-letter queue is retried forever and blocks its whole partition.
keyPoints.quote: job that always crashes is retried forever and blocks its partition

keyPoints.text: [w3] Slow jobs outlive their lease, a second worker picks the job up, and the slow first worker must be stopped from committing a stale result (a fencing token).
keyPoints.quote: a fencing token stops the slow first worker from committing a stale result

keyPoints.text: [w2] One tenant's flood starves everyone else unless queues are bounded and limits are per tenant.
keyPoints.quote: Bounded queues and per-tenant limits stop one customer's flood from starving everyone

keyPoints.text: [w2] A failing downstream plus naive retries turns a blip into a self-inflicted outage; backoff and jitter spread the retries out.
keyPoints.quote: retries without backoff and jitter turn a blip into a self-inflicted outage

keyPoints.text: [w2] Priority scheduling under load starves the low-priority jobs; the design says what guarantees they still get.
[w1] The dead-letter queue fills silently unless someone owns it and redrives it.
keyPoints.quote: someone must look at the DLQ

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your job-queue choices against the alternatives the guide names. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] At-least-once plus dedupe over at-most-once: at-most-once loses jobs on failure; effectively-once costs storage for seen ids and a retention window, which the answer sizes.
keyPoints.quote: storage for seen ids, a retention window

keyPoints.text: [w2] Enqueue via an outbox makes the producer's DB change and the job appear together, paying for a relay and at-least-once delivery.
[w2] Asynchronous by design: the queue buys decoupling and resilience and costs delay, which background work tolerates.
[w2] Hash-partitioned jobs vs one global queue: per-key order and scale-out, but adding partitions later reshuffles keys and breaks per-key order.
[w1] Prefer boring: a database table as the queue covers most products; a dedicated log or broker comes in when the numbers force it, and the answer shows those numbers.
keyPoints.quote: Reach for sharding, event sourcing or consensus when the numbers force you
